opus-5.5.text:
I think the core principle for us is that ownership comes with real authority. Each of the four of us has a fairly clear area: someone owns the core inference engine and systems work, someone owns research direction, someone owns the business and partnerships side, and so on. When one person has a firm view on something squarely within their area, the default is that we trust them and they make the call.

That doesn't mean the rest of us stay quiet. We argue a lot, actually. The norm is that anyone can push back, ask hard questions, and lay out the risks they see. But there's a difference between "I disagree and here's why" and "I'm going to block this." Once the owner has heard the arguments, if they still hold their view, we go with it. We call it something like "disagree and commit," which isn't original, but it works.

The reason is practical. In a startup, especially in infrastructure where things move very fast, the cost of slow decisions is often higher than the cost of a slightly wrong decision. If every choice needed consensus among four strong-minded people, we'd spend all our time in meetings. And the person who owns an area usually has the most context. They're the one looking at the benchmarks every day, talking to the customers, reading the code.

Of course there are exceptions. If something crosses areas, or it's an existential, company-level bet, like a major shift in direction or a big hire or fundraising decision, then we sit down together and try to reach real agreement. And if someone keeps making calls that turn out badly, that becomes a conversation about the ownership itself, not about one decision.

I'd also say that this only works because of trust built over a long time. Several of us knew each other from our academic and open-source work before starting the company, so we've seen how each other thinks under pressure. Without that foundation, I'm not sure any decision framework would really hold up.

r001.rationale: The response says that when a founder has a firm view on something within their area, they are trusted to make the call, even after hearing others’ arguments.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, we try to make that question come up as rarely as possible, because the four of us split responsibilities fairly cleanly from the start. If something falls squarely inside one person's area, the default is simple: that person decides. The rest of us can offer opinions, we can argue, but at the end of the day we respect that they have the context and they're the one who has to live with the consequences.

Where it gets interesting is when someone has a firm view and the rest of us disagree. My feeling is that a firm view is itself information. If one of us has thought about a problem for months and feels strongly, that conviction usually comes from somewhere, even if they can't fully articulate it in a meeting. So we tend not to vote. Voting among four people is a bad mechanism anyway, you just end up two against two. Instead we ask the person to lay out their reasoning as clearly as they can, and we ask the dissenters to be specific about what they think will go wrong. Very often that process alone resolves it, because either the owner spots a gap, or the rest of us realize our objection was vague.

If it still doesn't resolve, we go with the owner's judgment, and we agree in advance on what signal would tell us the decision was wrong. That matters more than the decision itself. It keeps the disagreement from turning into a personal thing and lets us revisit it with data instead of ego. And frankly, in a startup speed matters more than being right on every single call. A decisive wrong decision that we can correct in two weeks is better than a correct decision we debated for two months.

The one exception is anything that affects the whole company's direction, like what we build, who we hire at the senior level, how we raise money. Those aren't anyone's "area," so there we insist on genuine consensus, even if it takes longer. But for the day-to-day, trusting each other's ownership is really the only way four technical people can work together without driving each other crazy.

r001.rationale: The response says that when a matter falls within a founder’s area, that founder decides by default, and that unresolved disagreements defer to the owner’s judgment.

astra-6.text: I think the key is that responsibility and decision-making authority should go together. The four of us can discuss a decision and challenge each other’s assumptions, but if someone is responsible for that area and has a strong conviction, we should generally let that person make the call. Otherwise, it’s hard to hold anyone accountable. That doesn’t mean every decision will be right—we still need to look at the results and adjust—but we don’t need all four founders to agree on every detail.

r001.rationale: The response says that when a founder responsible for an area has a strong conviction, they should generally make the call, without requiring all four founders to agree.

sol-6.1.text: The four of us each have our own areas of responsibility. If someone has a strong view within their area, we discuss it and share our concerns, but ultimately we respect that person’s judgment. Otherwise, responsibility becomes unclear—you can’t ask someone to own the outcome while denying them the authority to make the decision. That doesn’t mean we always agree, but once a decision is made, we work together to carry it out.

r001.rationale: The response says the founders ultimately respect the responsible founder’s judgment and that they have authority to make the decision in their area.
